Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Kurus, in a market town of the Kuru people named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks." "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "This is the direct path <note>original: "ekāyano maggo"</note>, monks, for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the passing away of pain and distress, for the attainment of the method, and for the realization of <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>extinguishment/liberation</gloss>: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and distress regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and distress regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and distress regarding the world. He dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and distress regarding the world.

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk having gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down cross-legged, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness before him. Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows, 'I am breathing in long'; or breathing out long, he knows, 'I am breathing out long.' Breathing in short, he knows, 'I am breathing in short'; or breathing out short, he knows, 'I am breathing out short.' He trains, 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains, 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains, 'I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation'; he trains, 'I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.'

<summary>This text introduces the Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, detailing the direct path to liberation through the four foundations of mindfulness, beginning with the practice of mindful breathing.</summary>
<keywords>Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, mindfulness, four foundations, breath meditation, liberation</keywords>
